## Slide 1

Smashing into the Nucleus.

Particle accelerators speed up charged particles to high energies so they can probe the structure of matter.

Our big question for this lesson: how do scientists discover particles they can't see? The first physicists to probe the nucleus with fast particles had to use particles from radioactive sources, or cosmic rays from space, which they didn't yet understand.

In the early 1930s, scientists built laboratory machines that could accelerate protons and alpha particles to energies high enough to break into the nucleus. Today, linear accelerators and synchrotrons regularly push particles to huge energies, helping scientists uncover more and more about what matter is made of.

## Slide 3

Linear Accelerators.

A linear accelerator speeds up charged particles through a series of hollow tubes whose alternating potential difference reverses as the particles pass.

A linear accelerator can speed up protons, electrons, or their antimatter partners. It's a line of hollow tubes inside a long vacuum chamber, wired to a high-frequency alternating potential difference, as in Figure 16. Protons come from an ion source. When the first tube is negative, protons accelerate into it. Inside the tube there's no electric field, so they coast at constant velocity.

The tube length and the frequency are tuned so that the potential flips just as the protons reach the far end. Now the next tube is negative compared to the first, and the field in the gap pushes the protons forward again. Since the protons go faster after every gap, they travel farther in the same time, so each tube must be longer than the last. The protons ride the crest of an electric field wave like a surfer on the ocean, gaining about ten to the fifth electron volts at each gap, and can end up with billions of electron volts. Only charged particles can be accelerated this way.

Stanford University's linear accelerator is 3.3 kilometers long and gives electrons energies of 50 giga electron volts. Protons, though, are usually sped up in linear accelerators only as a first step before being injected into circular accelerators, where they reach much higher energies.

## Slide 4

Synchrotrons.

A synchrotron is a circular accelerator in which bending magnets steer particles around a ring and alternating electric fields accelerate them.

Steering particles in a circle with a magnetic field makes an accelerator more compact. A circular accelerator, called a synchrotron, is shown in Figure 17. Bending magnets are separated by straight sections where a high-frequency potential difference speeds the particles up.

The magnetic field strength and the path length are chosen so the particles arrive at each accelerating section exactly when the field's polarity will push them forward. Lap after lap, they gain more and more energy.

## Slide 5

The Large Hadron Collider.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN is a synchrotron 27 kilometers around in which two proton beams travel in opposite directions and collide.

One of the biggest synchrotrons is the Large Hadron Collider, or LHC, at the European Organization for Nuclear Research, CERN, near Geneva, Switzerland. Its ring is 27 kilometers around! It's that big because it takes a long distance to push particles to the energies scientists want.

The LHC has two proton beams racing in opposite directions. They collide in several interaction regions, and scientists study the results. The LHC can also accelerate larger nuclei.

## Slide 6

Detecting the Invisible.

Particles can be detected when they expose photographic film, ionize matter, or cause matter to emit photons.

When fast particles collide or crash into targets, they make a spray of subatomic particles. To detect a particle, it has to interact with matter in a way people can observe. Your hand will stop an alpha particle, and you'd never know it! And trillions of neutrinos, many from the Sun, pass through your body undetected every second.

Over the past century, scientists invented ways to catch these particles in the act. Remember that radiation from uranium exposes photographic film? Alpha, beta, and gamma radiation all do that, so film is a useful detector. Fast particles can also knock electrons off atoms, ionizing matter. And some substances give off photons when radiation hits them. Those are the three ways shown in Figure 18.

## Slide 7

Geiger-Muller Tubes.

A Geiger-Muller tube detects radiation when an ionized gas atom sets off an avalanche of charged particles and a pulse of current.

A Geiger-Muller tube has a negatively charged copper cylinder with a positively charged wire running down its center. The potential difference between them is held just below the point where a spark would jump on its own.

When a charged particle or gamma ray enters, it ionizes a gas atom. The positive ion speeds toward the cylinder and the electron toward the wire. Along the way they knock loose more charges, making an avalanche, and a pulse of current flows through the tube. That's the click you hear! Geiger counters are useful because they're small enough to carry around.

## Slide 8

Cloud and Bubble Chambers.

In cloud and bubble chambers, charged particles leave trails of ions that form visible droplets or bubbles.

An older detector, the Wilson cloud chamber, held air supersaturated with water or ethanol vapor. Charged particles zipping through left trails of ions, and vapor condensed into tiny droplets on those ions, making visible trails. In a bubble chamber, charged particles pass through a liquid held just above its boiling point, and the ion trails make tiny vapor bubbles, marking the paths, as in Figure 19.

Why do the trails bend in different directions? A magnetic field around the chamber pushes positive and negative particles opposite ways, so their tracks curve opposite ways. Neutral particles leave no trails at all, because they don't ionize the material. But scientists can use conservation of energy and momentum in collisions to infer that a neutral particle was there.

## Slide 9

Modern Detectors and ATLAS.

Modern detectors such as wire chambers, solid-state detectors, and light-emitting detectors record particle paths and measure momentum, mass, and energy.

Today's detectors record particle paths and measure momentum, mass, and energy. A wire chamber works like a giant Geiger-Muller tube: big plates separated by a small gap of low-pressure gas. A passing particle makes a discharge, and a computer records where. Solid-state detectors also track particles by ionization, and other detectors give off light when particles pass through, often to measure energy or momentum.

These detector arrays can be enormous. ATLAS at the Large Hadron Collider, in Figure 20, is 25 meters high and is really many detectors working together. It's designed to monitor a billion collisions each second and pick out about 100 that may interest scientists. The data become computer pictures of the collisions, like this June 2012 proton-proton collision from the search for the Higgs boson, where red tracks show two pairs of muons.

Compared with a Wilson cloud chamber, where scientists photographed visible droplet trails, ATLAS uses electronic detectors and computers to track, measure, and sort huge numbers of particles at once.

## Slide 10

The Neutrino Puzzle.

The neutrino, "little neutral one," is a neutral, nearly massless particle emitted along with the beta particle in beta decay.

In 1930, the atom looked simple: protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Then radioactive decay threw in a puzzle. Alpha particles and gamma rays come out with single, definite energies that depend on the decaying nucleus. But beta particles come out with a wide range of energies, often less than the energy the nucleus lost.

Where did the missing energy go? Niels Bohr even wondered whether energy might not be conserved. Instead, Wolfgang Pauli, around 1930 and 1931, and Enrico Fermi, in 1934, proposed that an unseen neutral particle was carrying the missing energy out along with the beta particle. Fermi named it the neutrino, Italian for "little neutral one." That's a fitting name, since it has no charge and very little mass. The particle in beta minus decay is actually an antineutrino, and it wasn't directly detected until 1956.

## Slide 11

A Particle Zoo.

Accelerator experiments revealed many particles with a wide range of masses, charges, and lifetimes.

More particles kept turning up. The muon, which seemed like a heavy electron, was found in 1937. The pion was discovered in 1947. Then accelerator experiments revealed even more, with all sorts of masses. Some were far more massive than the proton. Some had charge and some were neutral. Some lasted as little as ten to the negative twenty-third seconds, while others never seemed to decay at all.

Keeping track of them all was tough. Once, when Fermi was asked to identify a particle track, he joked, "If I could remember the names of all these particles, I'd be a botanist!"

## Slide 12

Antimatter.

An antiparticle has the same mass and charge magnitude as its particle, but the opposite sign of charge; together, antiparticles are antimatter.

In the late 1920s, Paul Dirac predicted that every kind of particle has a partner antiparticle. The antiparticle has the same mass and the same size of charge, but the opposite sign. Together, these antiparticles are called antimatter, and sometimes they're written with a bar over the symbol.

In 1932, the electron's positive partner, the positron, was discovered. When a positron and an electron collide, they can annihilate each other and produce gamma rays, as in Figure 21. Other particles and their antiparticles do the same thing.

## Slide 13

The Standard Model, Quarks and Leptons.

The Standard Model is the theory explaining the interactions of the elementary particles, which are grouped into quarks, leptons, and bosons.

By the late 1960s, it was clear that protons, neutrons, and pions aren't fundamental, or elementary, particles. Physicists sort elementary particles into three families: quarks, leptons, and bosons, shown in Figure 22. The theory explaining how they interact is the Standard Model.

Quarks have mass and charge, feel the strong force, and combine into bigger particles called hadrons. There are six types, or flavors. Protons and neutrons are made of three quarks and are called baryons. A meson, like the pion, is one quark and one antiquark.

Leptons, like electrons and neutrinos, are elementary particles too, but a different family. They have mass, and some, like the electron, have charge, while neutrinos are neutral. There are six flavors of leptons. The big difference: unlike quarks, leptons don't feel the strong force.

## Slide 14

Bosons and Force Carriers.

Force carriers are particles that transmit forces between objects interacting at a distance.

Bosons, unlike quarks and leptons, don't obey the Pauli exclusion principle. That means more than one boson can be in the same quantum state at the same place and time. Elementary bosons come in two kinds: gauge bosons, which carry forces, and scalar bosons.

In 1935, Japanese physicist Hideki Yukawa proposed a particle that could carry the strong force through space. That grew into the idea of force carriers, particles that transmit forces between interacting objects. Photons carry the electromagnetic force. Gluons carry the strong force that binds quarks into hadrons. The W plus, W minus, and Z zero bosons carry the weak force involved in beta decay. The graviton is the name for the not-yet-detected carrier of gravity.

The only elementary scalar boson is the Higgs boson, an excitation of the Higgs field. Interactions with the Higgs field give elementary particles their masses. Composite particles are different: a proton's mass is about 938 million electron volts, and the masses its three quarks get from the Higgs field add up to only about 1 percent of that. The rest comes from the energy of the strong force that binds the quarks.

## Slide 15

Inside Protons and Neutrons.

A proton is two up quarks and one down quark, uud; a neutron is one up quark and two down quarks, udd.

Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks, as in Figure 23. An up quark, u, has a charge of plus two thirds e, and a down quark, d, has a charge of negative one third e.

A proton is uud. Its charge is plus two thirds plus two thirds minus one third, which equals plus one e. A neutron is udd. Its charge is plus two thirds minus one third minus one third, which equals zero. Notice that quarks have fractional charges, but the particles they make have whole-number charges.

You'll never see a free quark. The strong force holding quarks together gets stronger as you pull them apart, like a spring, unlike the electric force, which weakens with distance.

## Slide 16

Antiquarks and Antibaryons.

Every quark and lepton has an antiparticle with identical mass and, if charged, opposite charge.

Every quark and every lepton has its own antiparticle. A particle and its antiparticle have identical masses, and charged ones have opposite charges. An up quark has a charge of plus two thirds, so an anti-up quark has negative two thirds.

A baryon is three quarks, so its antiparticle is three antiquarks. A proton, uud, has a charge of plus 1. An antiproton is made of anti-up, anti-up, and anti-down, with a charge of negative two thirds minus two thirds plus one third, or negative 1. An antineutron is anti-up, anti-down, anti-down, with a charge of zero. A meson is a quark-antiquark pair, so its antiparticle is also a quark-antiquark pair.

## Slide 17

Annihilation Energy.

When a particle and its antiparticle annihilate, the energy released is E equals m times the square of c.

When a particle and its antiparticle annihilate, you can find the energy released with E equals m times the square of c. An electron and a positron can collide and make two gamma rays. Each has a mass of 9.11 times ten to the negative thirty-first kilograms.

The energy equivalent of the pair is E equals 2 times 9.11 times ten to the negative thirty-first kilograms, times the square of 3.00 times ten to the eighth meters per second. That's 1.64 times ten to the negative thirteenth joules. Converting with 1 electron volt equals 1.60 times ten to the negative nineteenth joules gives 1.02 times ten to the sixth electron volts, or 1.02 mega electron volts.

So when an electron and a positron at rest annihilate, the gamma rays they produce have a total energy of 1.02 mega electron volts.

## Slide 18

Pair Production.

Pair production is the conversion of energy into a matter-antimatter pair of particles.

Annihilation can run in reverse: energy can turn directly into matter! Turning energy into a matter-antimatter pair is called pair production. If a gamma ray with at least 1.02 mega electron volts passes close to a nucleus, it can become an electron and a positron.

Figure 24 shows this in a bubble chamber. A magnetic field made the oppositely charged tracks curl in opposite directions. The gamma rays, coming in from the top, are uncharged and leave no tracks. Any gamma-ray energy above 1.02 mega electron volts becomes kinetic energy of the pair. The positron soon meets another electron, and they annihilate into two or three gamma rays with a total energy of at least 1.02 mega electron volts.

Protons and neutrons are about 1800 times as massive as electrons, so making proton-antiproton or neutron-antineutron pairs takes much more energy. The first proton-antiproton pair was made and observed at Berkeley, California, in 1955.

## Slide 19

Particle Conservation.

Quarks and leptons are created or destroyed only in particle-antiparticle pairs, so the net number of each stays constant.

The net number of quarks and the net number of leptons in the universe stay constant. Quarks and leptons are only created or destroyed in particle-antiparticle pairs. Force carriers, like photons, gluons, weak bosons, and gravitons, are different: they can be created or destroyed if there's enough energy.

A gamma ray can't turn into just an electron, or just a positron, because that would break conservation of charge. And a gamma ray can't become an electron plus a proton either, even though the charges cancel. The pair has to be a particle and its own antiparticle.

## Slide 20

Beta Decay and the Weak Force.

The weak nuclear force is the interaction that acts in the nucleus during beta decay.

Neutrons in a stable nucleus don't decay, but free neutrons and neutrons in unstable nuclei can. In beta decay, a neutron becomes a proton by emitting a beta particle and an antineutrino. The antineutrino is uncharged with a tiny mass, but like a photon it carries momentum and energy. The equation: a neutron yields a proton plus an electron plus an antineutrino.

Protons can decay in a similar way. A free proton has never been seen to decay, but a proton inside a nucleus can become a neutron by emitting a positron and a neutrino. That's positron emission: a proton yields a neutron plus a positron plus a neutrino.

The strong force can't explain these decays, so there must be another interaction in the nucleus. It's called the weak nuclear force, and, as you might guess, it's much weaker than the strong force.

## Slide 21

The Quark Model of Beta Decay.

In beta decay, a down quark changes to an up quark by emitting a W minus boson, which then decays into an electron and an antineutrino.

A proton, uud, and a neutron, udd, differ by just one quark. Beta decay happens in two steps, shown in Figure 25. First, a d quark changes into a u quark by emitting a W minus boson, one of the three carriers of the weak force. Second, the W minus boson decays into an electron and an antineutrino.

What charge must the W minus have? The d quark has negative one third, and the u quark has plus two thirds. For charge to balance, the W minus must carry a charge of negative 1, just like the electron it becomes.

A proton in a nucleus can also turn into a neutron and a W plus boson. The W plus then decays into a positron and a neutrino.

## Slide 22

The Z Boson and Neutrino Mass.

The Z zero boson carries a weak interaction that does not change one quark into another.

The third weak-force carrier, the Z zero boson, is emitted without any quark changing into another. It produces an interaction between nucleons and the electrons in atoms that's similar to, but much weaker than, the electromagnetic force that holds atoms together. This interaction was first detected in the 1970s, and the W plus, W minus, and Z zero bosons were first observed directly in 1983.

Neutrinos were long thought to be massless. But experiments detecting neutrinos from the Sun show they do have mass. Their masses are far smaller than any other known particle's and haven't been measured accurately yet.

## Slide 23

Testing the Standard Model.

Interactions with the Higgs field determine the masses of the elementary particles.

Look at Figure 22 again. Quarks and leptons are split into three columns, or generations. The everyday world is made from the left-hand column: up quarks, down quarks, and electrons, which build protons, neutrons, and atoms. The middle column turns up in cosmic rays and is routinely made in accelerators. The right-hand column is thought to have existed briefly in the earliest moments of the Big Bang and is created in high-energy collisions.

What sets the masses of the quarks and leptons? In 2012, physicists observed the Higgs boson, with a mass of about 125 billion electron volts, at the Large Hadron Collider, confirming the long-predicted Higgs field. Interactions with that field determine an elementary particle's mass. With the Higgs field confirmed, the Standard Model, which explains how elementary particles interact through the fundamental forces, now explains where their mass comes from.

## Slide 24

Why Four Forces?

The four fundamental forces are the gravitational force, the electromagnetic force, the weak nuclear force, and the strong nuclear force.

The four fundamental forces are clearly different. They act on different things, like charge or mass. They change with distance in different ways. And their force carriers have different properties, as Figure 26 shows.

But there are similarities too. Photons carry the electromagnetic force in much the same way that weak bosons carry the weak force. The electromagnetic force reaches far because the photon has zero mass, while the weak force acts only over short distances because the W and Z bosons are fairly massive. And the mathematical structures of the two theories are similar.

## Slide 25

The Electroweak Force.

At extremely high energies, the electromagnetic and weak forces are unified into a single force called the electroweak force.

According to present theories of the universe's origin, the electromagnetic and weak forces were identical in the earliest moments of the cosmos, when energies were incredibly high. That's why they're said to be unified into a single force, the electroweak force, a theory developed in the 1970s.

Supernovas connect particle physics to the stars, too. Figure 27 shows supernova 1987A before and after it exploded, plus a close-up. The explosion gave off a burst of neutrinos along with its light. The neutrinos reached Earth about three hours before the light, because they escaped the collapsing core right away. That showed neutrinos are produced in supernovas and travel at nearly the speed of light.

Physicists are now working on theories that bring in the strong force as well. The work isn't finished: hypotheses are being revised, and experiments are being planned to test them. A fully unified theory that includes gravity will take even more effort.

## Slide 26

Dark Matter and Dark Energy.

Dark matter interacts with ordinary matter only through gravity; dark energy is thought to accelerate the universe's expansion.

Studies of galaxies are even more puzzling. They suggest that the matter described by the Standard Model makes up only a small fraction of the mass in the universe. Much more is dark matter, so called because it doesn't interact with light or ordinary matter except through gravity. And there seems to be dark energy, thought to be causing the universe's expansion to speed up.

So the study of the tiniest particles is tied directly to the study of the biggest things, the galaxies that fill the universe. Particle physicists and cosmologists used to work at opposite ends of the size scale. Now they're working together on the same question: what is the universe made of?

## Slide 27

Engineering and Technology, Fusion as a Future Energy Source.

Fusion could supply clean, abundant energy, but starting and sustaining a controlled fusion reaction is a major technological challenge.

Nuclear fusion could give Earth's growing population clean, sustainable, and abundant energy. In fusion, light nuclei combine into a larger nucleus and release a vast amount of energy, just as in the Sun. The fuel, forms of hydrogen, is available on Earth in huge amounts. Fusion produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, the process that powers today's nuclear plants, and it's safer. And the energy released is enormous.

So why aren't we using it yet? Starting and keeping a controlled fusion reaction going is really hard. The nuclei need very high thermal energy to overcome their repulsion. Temperatures above 150 million degrees Celsius are needed, and the superheated material, called plasma, must be held by electromagnets so it never touches, and melts, the reactor walls. With today's technology, reaching those temperatures usually takes more energy than the reaction gives back. Once fusion gets going, energy from the reactions can help keep the plasma hot, and then the challenge is sustaining and controlling it.

There are economic, political, and time challenges too. Fusion reactors take years of work, lots of space and money, and cooperation among many groups. That's the challenge of replicating the Sun here on Earth!
